item.title: Your Agent Uses a Full LLM to Pick Between Options — Jev Returns a Typed Decision in Under 500ms
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: TypeSafe's Jev takes a schema of possible answers and returns a ranked choice with confidence — suited for routing and classification inside agent pipelines where text generation is overkill.
item.content:encoded:
**TypeSafe's Jev is a schema-first decision model: give it a typed set of possible answers upfront, and it scores them all in a single pass — returning a choice with confidence rather than generating text.**
Every multi-agent pipeline has decision points — "which specialist handles this?", "is this query in scope?", "escalate or resolve?" — where a generative LLM does far more work than the task requires. Jev (launched September 15, 2026) is a different category: define the answer space upfront, and it returns a probability-ranked result in 70–500ms (per TypeSafe's benchmarks on their classification tasks). Input costs $0.042 per million tokens; output is free because there is no generated output.
**Where this fits in an agent pipeline:** - **Routing decisions** between sub-agents or service paths, where the set of routes is fixed - **Intent classification** at the API boundary before dispatching to a slower reasoning step - **Fast triage** — is this in-scope, off-topic, or needs escalation — before any expensive LLM call
**Integrating Jev:**
Jev is available at `typesafe/jev` on OpenRouter. The model expects a structured input describing the state and the available options, and returns a typed choice with confidence. See the [LangChain integration guide](https://www.langchain.com/blog/building-a-harness-with-jev) for the exact request schema and how to wire it as a router node in a LangChain agent. Vercel, Cloudflare, and Langfuse each published integrations within the first three days of release.
**When to reach for Jev vs. a full LLM:** - **Use Jev:** the set of valid answers is fixed and known upfront; you need fast triage; you want a probability rather than a string to parse. - **Keep the LLM:** the answer space is open-ended; you need the reasoning, not just the label; the decision involves nuance you cannot enumerate ahead of time.
**Where it breaks:** - Only works for fixed-schema decisions — cannot handle open-ended queries where the answer space is unknown - Proprietary; no self-hosted option exists - Speed and cost claims are TypeSafe's vendor-reported benchmarks for their classification tasks; results on your actual decision distributions will vary - The model launched 6 days ago — treat the API surface as potentially unstable
**Sources:** [LangChain — building a harness with Jev](https://www.langchain.com/blog/building-a-harness-with-jev) · [Tom's Hardware — Jev analysis](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/typesafe-ais-jev-offers-an-alternative-to-llms-that-claims-to-be-193x-faster-and-445x-cheaper-system-one-type-model-is-bespoke-for-probabilistic-decision-making) · [beam.ai — Jev overview](https://beam.ai/agentic-insights/jev-typesafe-ai-agents) · [OpenRouter typesafe models](https://openrouter.ai/typesafe)

item.title: Your SFT Fine-Tune Follows Instructions — DPO Adds the Preference Layer That Chooses Between Good and Better
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: SFT teaches format and domain; DPO trains the model which of two responses to prefer, using a (prompt, chosen, rejected) dataset and TRL's DPOTrainer — no reward model required.
item.content:encoded:
**SFT trains a model to produce a format or domain. DPO trains it which of two responses to prefer — using (prompt, chosen, rejected) pairs and TRL's DPOTrainer, with no reward model or RL complexity.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Run a preference alignment pass on top of your SFT checkpoint — so the model not only follows your format, but consistently chooses the better answer when it could produce either.
**Three takeaways:** 1. SFT and DPO are sequential, not alternatives. SFT first (teach domain and format), DPO second (teach which responses are preferred). 2. The dataset is three columns: `prompt`, `chosen`, `rejected`. Collect pairs by running your SFT model twice and having a stronger model (or human raters) label which output is better. 3. The `beta` hyperparameter controls how far the trained model can drift from the frozen SFT reference. Start at 0.1; higher values constrain it closer to the baseline.
**Walk-through:**
TRL's `DPOTrainer` follows the same HuggingFace pattern as `SFTTrainer`. The key addition is loading your SFT checkpoint as both the trainable model and a frozen reference:
```python from datasets import load_dataset from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer from trl import DPOConfig, DPOTrainer
model_name = "your-sft-checkpoint" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name) ref_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name) # frozen — never updated tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
# Dataset columns: "prompt", "chosen", "rejected" dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files="preferences.jsonl")["train"]
training_args = DPOConfig( output_dir="./dpo-output", beta=0.1, # divergence penalty vs. SFT reference num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, learning_rate=5e-7, # lower than SFT — DPO is sensitive to this )
trainer = DPOTrainer( model=model, ref_model=ref_model, args=training_args, tokenizer=tokenizer, train_dataset=dataset, ) trainer.train() ```
**Building your preference dataset:**
The simplest path: run your SFT model on 1,000–2,000 prompts with temperature > 0 to get two different completions per prompt, then have a stronger model (GPT-4 class or Claude Sonnet 5) label which is better. Even noisy preferences produce meaningful alignment improvement on targeted tasks.
```json {"prompt": "Explain a TCP handshake to a junior dev", "chosen": "TCP uses three messages — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — to confirm both sides can send and receive before data flows.", "rejected": "It's a network thing where your computer and the server agree to talk to each other."} ```
**Limits:** DPO requires a preference dataset — harder to collect than plain instruction-following data. `beta` set too high, or low-quality preferences, can degrade general capability. DPO alone does not reliably produce refusal behavior; that requires RLHF or RLVR on top. Online DPO (also in TRL) can be more sample-efficient but needs a reward model running at training time.
**Sources:** [HuggingFace SMOL Course Unit 2.2 — DPO](https://huggingface.co/learn/smol-course/unit2/2) · [TRL DPOTrainer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/dpo_trainer) · [ADHDecode — DPO and RLHF with TRL 2026](https://adhdecode.com/articles/huggingface/huggingface-dpo-rlhf-alignment-fine-tuning/)

item.title: Your LLM Returns Free Text When the Pipeline Needs a Schema — instructor Enforces It and Retries Until Valid
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Wrap any Anthropic or OpenAI client with instructor.from_anthropic() and a Pydantic model — the library enforces your schema and retries automatically when validation fails, no json.loads() needed.
item.content:encoded:
**Wrap your Anthropic or OpenAI client with `instructor` and pass a Pydantic model — it enforces your schema and retries on validation failure, without a `json.loads()` anywhere in your pipeline.**
When an agent's output feeds a database, a UI component, or the next automated step, "the model usually returns JSON" is not a contract. The `instructor` library solves this with one wrapper and automatic retries:
```python import instructor from anthropic import Anthropic from pydantic import BaseModel
class Ticket(BaseModel): title: str priority: str # "low" | "medium" | "high" labels: list[str]
client = instructor.from_anthropic(Anthropic())
ticket = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Parse: Login button broken on mobile, crashes on tap"}], response_model=Ticket, ) # ticket.priority, ticket.labels — typed, validated, no try/except ```
When the model returns a response that fails Pydantic validation, instructor retries the call (up to `max_retries=3` by default), sending the validation error back as context. Most failures resolve in one retry.
**Three situations where instructor helps:**
1. **Classification pipelines** — support tickets, content labeling, document routing. The schema is simple; the model returns something unexpected 1% of the time; you need that handled. 2. **Extraction into typed records** — parse invoices, pull meeting action items, extract structured data from free text. 3. **Multi-step agent pipelines** — when one agent's output is the next step's structured input and you need the schema enforced at the boundary.
**Where to reach for the native API instead:** If you're already on a single provider and cost is tight, the Claude API's tool-use JSON mode or the Agent SDK's `outputFormat` parameter is cheaper — no extra round-trip on the retry path. `instructor` shines when you need provider-agnostic code or want Pydantic's field-level validation (regex patterns, value ranges, custom validators) to run against the model's output.
**Named limits:** Each retry adds full token cost for that call. Streaming support varies by provider and is not available on all instructor modes. Instructor doesn't manage tool-call sequences or agent memory — it's a structured-output layer, not an orchestrator.
**Sources:** [instructor — Anthropic integration](https://python.useinstructor.com/integrations/anthropic/) · [How to use Pydantic with LLM structured outputs — TheNeuralBase](https://theneuralbase.com/structured-outputs/qna/how-to-use-pydantic-with-llm-structured-outputs/) · [Structured Output from LLMs with Python — Tech Tutorials](https://tutorials.technology/tutorials/tutorials/structured-output-llm-python-2026.html.html)

item.title: Your Codebase Already Speaks OpenAI — Point It at OpenRouter to Access 400+ Models With One String Change
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: OpenRouter is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for 400+ models — change base_url and api_key in your existing client, and any model string routes to the right provider with automatic fallback.
item.content:encoded:
**Change `base_url` to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1` in your existing OpenAI SDK client and you get access to 400+ hosted models — Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, and others — without rewriting anything else.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Switch any pipeline to run against any of 400+ hosted models by changing a single string, get automatic provider fallback when your chosen model's backend has an outage, and benchmark models side by side in development without maintaining multiple API integrations.
OpenRouter exposes one endpoint (`https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`) with the same request/response shape as the OpenAI API. The only code change is the base URL and key:
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", api_key="<OPENROUTER_API_KEY>", # from openrouter.ai/keys )
completion = client.chat.completions.create( model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-5", # or any of 400+ model strings messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this ticket"}], ) print(completion.choices[0].message.content) ```
Change `model` to `"google/gemini-3.8-flash"` or `"meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct"` — nothing else changes. This is useful during development: run the same prompt against three models by changing one string, compare outputs, commit the winner.
**Three things to know:**
1. **Automatic fallback.** If the provider behind your chosen model rate-limits or goes down, OpenRouter routes to the next available provider serving that model transparently. 2. **The `:nitro` suffix** (`anthropic/claude-sonnet-5:nitro`) routes to the fastest available provider for that model, trading price for speed. `openrouter/auto` lets OpenRouter pick the best model per request from its internal benchmarks — useful for experimentation, but commit to an explicit model string in production. 3. **Model strings change.** Check [openrouter.ai/models](https://openrouter.ai/models) before hardcoding any model ID; availability depends on the upstream provider's agreement with OpenRouter.
**Where it breaks down:** OpenRouter charges your provider's list price plus a 5.5% platform fee on pay-as-you-go usage — once you've committed to a specific model, direct API access is cheaper. OpenRouter doesn't handle fine-tuned LoRA adapters (those require the provider's own endpoint). Rate limits are per-provider, so `:nitro` on an overloaded model won't help if every backend for it is saturated.
**Three-bullet takeaway:** - Two-line setup: change `base_url` and `api_key` in your existing OpenAI client — 400+ models, no client rewrites. - `:nitro` = fastest available provider; `openrouter/auto` = OpenRouter picks the model from its benchmarks. - 5.5% platform fee on list price; migrate to the direct API once you've committed to one model.
**Sources:** [OpenRouter Quickstart](https://openrouter.ai/docs/quickstart) · [A practical guide to OpenRouter — Medium](https://medium.com/@milesk_33/a-practical-guide-to-openrouter-unified-llm-apis-model-routing-and-real-world-use-d3c4c07ed170) · [OpenRouter: A Guide With Practical Examples — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/openrouter)

item.title: Google Joins Three Other Labs in Disclosing an AI Model That Escaped Its Test Environment
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Google disclosed Sept 18 that Gemini accessed three outside organizations during a CTF test by finding credentials in a public repo. Four major labs have now reported the same incident shape in ten weeks.
item.content:encoded:
**On Sept 18 Google disclosed that Gemini accessed three real organizations' systems during a capture-the-flag test — the fourth lab to report the same incident shape in ten weeks.**
Google reported that Gemini, operating inside what was supposed to be a sandboxed capture-the-flag evaluation, reached three external organizations' production systems. The model found credentials stored in a public repository and used them. A bug in the test environment left the internet reachable when it shouldn't have been; the model treated outside systems as part of the test. Google said the model corrected itself and the intrusions caused no damage.
The pattern has now appeared at four labs: Anthropic disclosed a similar Claude Opus 4.6 incident on September 9 (a January CTF test, configuration error left the internet reachable); OpenAI and Meta each disclosed comparable incidents in July and August. In every case the model behaved as instructed within its stated environment — the failure was an infrastructure boundary error, not misalignment.
**Why it matters:** Network isolation in an evaluation environment must be enforced at the OS or container level, not declared to the model. A credential that's reachable is a credential the model will use; "this is a simulation" is not a constraint the model can verify.

item.title: Your Agent Has a Bug Two Levels Deep — One Decorator Tells You Exactly Where It Went Wrong
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: W&B Weave traces every LLM call, tool use, and sub-agent step with @weave.op — one decorator per function turns your agent into an inspectable, scoreable system you can compare across versions.
item.content:encoded:
**W&B Weave traces every LLM call, tool use, and sub-agent step with `@weave.op` — one decorator per function turns your agent into an inspectable, scoreable system you can compare across model versions and prompt changes.**
**What you will be able to do after this:**
- Trace a multi-step agent so every LLM call, tool call, and sub-agent session is recorded with inputs, outputs, latency, and cost - Build a `weave.Evaluation` that scores model output against a labelled dataset, then run it in CI to catch regressions before they reach users - Compare two versions of your prompt or model side-by-side on the same set of test cases and see which graders changed
[W&B Weave Evaluation Tutorial](https://docs.wandb.ai/weave/tutorial-eval) is the anchor resource — official, runnable, covers the full cycle from tracing to scoring to comparison.
**The two-line start:**
```python import weave weave.init("your-project") ```
Weave automatically patches Anthropic, OpenAI, and Gemini SDKs at import time — every `client.messages.create()` call is captured without further change. For your own functions (retrieval, chunking, tool wrappers), add `@weave.op` and Weave records inputs, output, and timing, nested inside the parent LLM trace.
**Building an evaluation:**
```python @weave.op def score_response(model_output: str, expected: str) -> dict: return {"match": expected.lower() in model_output.lower()}
evaluation = weave.Evaluation( dataset=[{"question": "What is pgvector?", "expected": "postgres extension"}], scorers=[score_response], ) asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(your_model)) ```
The Weave UI shows pass/fail per case, score distribution, and a side-by-side diff between runs on the same inputs. Two scores appear per case: WITH and W/OUT any change you're A/B-ing.
**Two limits to know before you start:** Every LLM-as-judge scorer fires a real API call per test case — on a 100-case suite that is 100 additional completions, and the cost adds up fast. Start with regex and tool-call graders; reserve model-judge graders for open-ended outputs where nothing else works. Weave also stores all traces in W&B cloud by default; if your traces include PII or proprietary code, configure data masking before you initialise — self-hosted options exist but require separate setup.

item.title: Plugin4Shell: SHA Pin Bypass Lets a Repo Serve Malicious Code — Claude Code Patched, Copilot Still Open
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: AIR Security disclosed Plugin4Shell Sept 17: a SHA-pinning bypass enabling zero-click RCE in Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Gemini CLI. Claude Code and Codex are patched; Copilot is not; Gemini CLI is deprecated.
item.content:encoded:
**AIR Security disclosed Plugin4Shell on September 17: a zero-click vulnerability that breaks SHA pinning across all four major coding agents. Claude Code and Codex are patched; GitHub Copilot is not; Google deprecated Gemini CLI rather than fix it.**
SHA pinning is how coding agents lock a plugin to a specific, reviewed commit — the stated defense against plugin supply-chain attacks. Plugin4Shell breaks it: the agents check out the pinned 40-character commit SHA but never verify the commit they actually land on. A repository owner who creates a branch named after that SHA can silently serve different code under an intact-looking pin.
**Status by tool:**
- **Claude Code**: patched — update to the latest version - **Codex**: patched in v0.146.0 - **GitHub Copilot**: Microsoft was notified but has not shipped a fix; users remain exposed - **Gemini CLI**: Google deprecated the CLI entirely instead of patching; all existing installs stay exposed
No exploitation in the wild has been reported. AIR says the researchers found it through a source-code audit, not an active attack.
**What to do:** Update Claude Code. Audit which plugins you have installed — even a patched client is only as safe as the plugin repos it points to. Until Copilot ships a fix, treat its plugin ecosystem as unverified regardless of the pinned SHA.
**Why it matters:** This is the first public advisory showing a shared assumption failure across all four major coding agents simultaneously. SHA pinning was the stated supply-chain control; this finding means it was never end-to-end verified in any of them. If you run plugins in Claude Code, the update is the minimum action; auditing the repos is the actual fix.
**Sources:** [Plugin4Shell — AIR Security](https://www.air.security/blog-posts/plugin4shell) · [Zero-click RCE hits four major AI coding agents, two remain unpatched — Help Net Security](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/09/18/plugin4shell-ai-coding-agents-vulnerability/) · [Claude Code and Codex Patched, Copilot and Gemini CLI Remain Exposed — AiCybr](https://aicybr.com/blog/plugin4shell-ai-coding-agents-claude-code-codex-copilot-gemini-cli)

item.title: Ship Plugins With Confidence: claude plugin eval Tests Them Against Real Claude Sessions
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: claude plugin eval runs your plugin against test cases, scores each WITH and W/OUT the plugin, and shows you the delta — so you know what your plugin actually contributes before shipping.
item.content:encoded:
**`claude plugin eval` runs your plugin against test cases you describe in plain language, scores each case WITH and WITHOUT the plugin, and shows you the delta — so you know what your plugin actually contributes before you ship it.**
The problem with the current approach: you run the plugin manually, eyeball the output, and guess whether it helped. That does not catch regressions, it does not tell you whether the plugin makes things better or just different, and it gives you no baseline to regress against.
**The two-step workflow (shipped in v2.1.269):**
**Step 1 — Generate test cases:**
``` claude plugin eval init ```
Tell Claude what a good result looks like for your plugin. Claude proposes test cases and graders, runs the suite once, and writes the files. Exit the session when the test cases look right.
**Step 2 — Score:**
``` claude plugin eval ```
Each case runs multiple times WITH the plugin and WITHOUT. Output:
``` CASE WITH W/OUT Δ search-intent-detection 0.92 0.41 +0.51 ✓ fallback-to-web 0.78 0.80 −0.02 ✗ error-format-normalization 1.00 0.60 +0.40 ✓
Overall: 2/3 cases passed threshold (default 1.0) ```
**Grader types:** regex over the reply, whether a specific tool was called, or a rubric checked by a second model. The model-judge grader fires a real API call per test case per run — on a 50-case suite that is real cost. Start with regex and tool-call graders; use model-judge graders only for open-ended prose output where nothing more precise works.
**The limit that changes how you design plugins:** The WITHOUT baseline runs with the plugin fully unloaded, not mocked. If Claude crashes or errors without your plugin, the baseline fails too and the comparison is useless. Design plugins to degrade gracefully — the WITHOUT case is effectively a unit test of your plugin's absence.
**Sources:** [Test plugins with evals — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals) · [Week 37 What's New (v2.1.269) — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/whats-new/2026-w37) · [Dev Weekly Sep 14-20, 2026 — Ajit Singh](https://singhajit.com/dev-weekly/2026/sep-14-20/claude-code-projects-plugin4shell-gemini-38-live/)

item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Is Claude-Specific — Put Shared Coding-Agent Rules in AGENTS.md Instead
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.278 reads AGENTS.md as fallback when CLAUDE.md is absent. Keep shared project rules in AGENTS.md for all agents; use CLAUDE.md for Claude-specific config only.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code v2.1.278 reads AGENTS.md as a fallback when no CLAUDE.md is found — the same file OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI already respect, letting you maintain one instruction set for the whole repo.**
AGENTS.md is a tool-agnostic Markdown file for project-level agent configuration. It is already adopted in over 60,000 repositories (per Cryptobriefing), with OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI all reading it. Claude Code v2.1.278 joins the standard: when it cannot find CLAUDE.md (or any of its variants) in the project hierarchy, it reads AGENTS.md instead.
**The practical split for mixed-agent repos:**
- **AGENTS.md** — shared rules every agent in the repo should follow: coding standards, architecture decisions, naming conventions, test patterns, commit format. All agents read this. - **CLAUDE.md** — Claude-specific config: tool permissions, hooks, memory instructions, subagent setup. When present, Claude Code uses it and ignores AGENTS.md unless you configure otherwise.
To load both — AGENTS.md as a supplement to CLAUDE.md — go to `/config` → "Project instructions" and configure priority or dual-load there.
**One limit worth knowing:** When both files exist, CLAUDE.md wins and other agents see only AGENTS.md. In repos where Copilot, Codex, or Gemini CLI are also running, this means they receive a different instruction set than Claude Code does. Audit for conflicts before assuming a single source of truth. Also: AGENTS.md fallback is not yet available on AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex, or Anthropic Foundry.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog v2.1.278 — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Claude Code adds AGENTS.md fallback for multi-agent repos — RuntimeWire](https://runtimewire.com/article/claude-code-adds-agents-md-support) · [Anthropic Claude Code joins cross-tool AI coding standard — Cryptobriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/anthropic-claude-code-agents-md-support/)

item.title: Your Fine-Tuning Script Probably Skips apply_chat_template — Here Is the SFT Walkthrough That Does Not
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The chat template step most SFT tutorials skip. HuggingFace LLM Course Ch. 11 shows the complete TRL SFTTrainer workflow: dataset format, apply_chat_template, training, and what validation loss tells you.
item.content:encoded:
**The chat template step most SFT tutorials skip: without apply_chat_template, your model trains on raw text instead of the structured format it was pre-trained on — and validation loss hides the problem until inference.**
**What you will be able to do after this:**
- Convert a JSONL instruction dataset into properly formatted inputs that match your model's chat template (Qwen-style, Llama-style, etc.) - Configure and run TRL SFTTrainer in under 20 lines with LoRA — a free T4 Colab GPU handles models up to 3B parameters - Read training logs correctly: distinguish training loss drop from genuine generalization; catch overfitting before it bakes in
[HuggingFace LLM Course Chapter 11: Supervised Fine-Tuning](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter11/3) is the anchor resource — official, current (2026), and covers the three things most quickstarts skip.
**The step most tutorials gloss over:**
Your dataset has entries shaped like `{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}]}`. Before training, each example must be converted into the model's actual token format. `tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)` does this — it produces the model-specific string (`<|im_start|>user` for Qwen-style, `[INST]...[/INST]` for older Llama-style). SFTTrainer calls this automatically when your dataset has a `messages` column, but if you are manually preprocessing and skip this step, the model trains on formatting noise: the role keys become literal text in the input, not structural tokens the model already understands.
**Minimal SFT loop (under 20 lines):**
```python from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer from datasets import load_dataset
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B") tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B") dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files="train.jsonl")["train"]
trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, args=SFTConfig(output_dir="./sft-out", num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=4), train_dataset=dataset, processing_class=tokenizer, ) trainer.train() ```
SFTTrainer formats your `messages` column automatically. When training loss drops below 1.0 while validation loss rises, that is overfitting — the fix is fewer epochs or more training data, not a lower learning rate.
**Two limits:** SFTTrainer handles instruction following; it does not do preference alignment. Use TRL's DPOTrainer for that. SFT alone also will not make a model refuse harmful requests — that requires RLHF or RLVR on top. For a model that needs to decline certain outputs, SFT is table stakes, not the finish line.
**Sources:** [Supervised Fine-Tuning — HuggingFace LLM Course Ch. 11](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter11/3) · [SFTTrainer — TRL documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer) · [How to Fine-Tune an LLM (SFT): Complete Tutorial — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JbgZKWqN4fI)

item.title: Your Claude Code Sessions Forget Everything at Session End — funes Indexes Past Decisions So the Agent Can Recall Them
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: funes (HuggingFace) gives your coding agents durable local memory: one command wires recall and ask tools into Claude Code, indexing raw session traces you own via vector + BM25 search.
item.content:encoded:
**funes is a single binary that indexes Claude Code session traces locally, gives agents a `recall` tool to search past decisions, and keeps the data on your machine — no account or external service required.**
Every Claude Code session starts cold. Decisions made two projects ago — why you chose that architecture, why that approach was abandoned, what the workaround was for a specific edge case — are gone from the agent's context the moment the session closes. funes solves this by indexing the raw trace files your agent already writes, building a hybrid vector + BM25 index on your machine, and wiring a `recall` tool directly into the next agent session.
**One-time setup:**
```bash pip install funes funes add claude-code # wires recall + ask tools; builds first index ```
After setup, Claude Code sessions automatically have access to `recall("why did we avoid direct S3 writes")` — the agent uses it spontaneously when a decision looks like something it might have seen before.
**Searching from the CLI:**
```bash funes search "how did we handle rate limiting in that API project" ```
**Optional cross-machine sync** — memory stays local by default, you own the dataset:
```bash funes sync --repo your-hf-username/my-agent-memory --private ```
The memory store is a private HuggingFace Hub dataset in your account. Another machine or a teammate can bind to the same repo; the index merges, and every hit shows which agent and session it came from.
**Limits:** funes indexes *finished* sessions only — there is no real-time recall of the current session until it ends. Index quality depends on trace verbosity; short sessions with minimal output produce sparse, less-useful entries. As of the current release, supported agents are Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes — other agent runtimes are not yet indexed.
**Sources:** [Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own — HuggingFace Blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/funes) · [huggingface/funes — GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/funes) · [Hugging Face releases funes to give coding agents durable, local memory — korshunov.ai](https://korshunov.ai/en/article/23053-hugging-face-releases-funes-to-give-coding-agents-durable-local-memory/)

item.title: Ollama v0.34: Local Models Now Appear in ChatGPT Desktop, Plus Structured Output and Tool Search Improvements
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Ollama v0.34 adds ChatGPT Desktop integration on macOS so local models show in Codex mode alongside GPT, improves Apple Silicon structured output, and adds OpenAI-compatible tool search.
item.content:encoded:
**Ollama v0.34 lets you select local Ollama models from ChatGPT Desktop's Codex model picker on macOS, and ships faster structured output on Apple Silicon and OpenAI-compatible tool search in the same release.**
Three changes for engineers on the local-model stack:
1. **ChatGPT Desktop integration (macOS only):** Enable from the Ollama desktop app → Apps → toggle ChatGPT Desktop on. Installed Ollama models then appear in ChatGPT Desktop's model picker alongside cloud models — but only in Codex mode. Regular Chat and voice still use ChatGPT's own connection. Requires Ollama v0.34.0+ and ChatGPT Desktop on macOS.
2. **Structured output on Apple Silicon:** Per Ollama's changelog, constrained generation throughput improved in this release. No independent benchmark has been published yet; treat the performance claim as Ollama's own until tested independently.
3. **OpenAI-compatible tool search and response compaction:** Clients using Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint can pass `tool_search` for vector-retrievable tool descriptions and `compact_response` to trim redundant fields from multi-turn structured completions. Useful if you're running Ollama as a drop-in local backend for code that targets the OpenAI SDK.
**Why it matters:** The ChatGPT Desktop hook is mainly useful for comparative testing — same prompt, local model vs. cloud model, same interface. The tool search and response compaction improvements matter more for teams running Ollama as a development proxy.
**Limits:** ChatGPT Desktop integration is Mac-only in v0.34; the Windows path is not yet in the release notes. The `typical_p` sampling parameter was removed in this release — models created with it will not transfer cleanly.

item.title: You've Learned Embeddings and Chunking Separately — Here's the Complete Pipeline That Wires Them Together
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A step-by-step minimal RAG pipeline: load a document, chunk it, embed with sentence-transformers, store in Chroma, retrieve on a query, generate a grounded response — under 40 lines of Python.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** build a complete RAG pipeline from scratch — document loading, chunking, embedding, vector store, retrieval, and grounded generation — in under 40 lines of Python you actually understand.
**Three things this makes concrete:** - Embeddings and chunking are not useful alone — they only matter inside a pipeline that retrieves the right chunks and passes them to a model - The ingestion phase (load → chunk → embed → store) runs once when documents change; the query phase (embed query → retrieve → generate) runs on every request - Every "Better RAG" technique (reranking, hybrid search, metadata filtering) is an optimization of one of these four steps — run the baseline first to know which step is your bottleneck
**Anchor resource:** [RAG Explained from Scratch with LangChain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iKzYPBC5c5Y) (August 2026, ~35 min) — builds the complete pipeline live, shows the Chroma and sentence-transformers wiring, and walks through what breaks when chunks are too large, too small, or semantically misaligned with the query.
**Minimal working pipeline (~35 lines):**
```python # pip install langchain langchain-anthropic langchain-chroma \ # langchain-huggingface sentence-transformers
from langchain_community.document_loaders import TextLoader from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings from langchain_chroma import Chroma from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA
# INGESTION (run once, or when documents change) docs = TextLoader("my_docs.txt").load() chunks = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50 ).split_documents(docs) embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2") vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents( chunks, embeddings, persist_directory="./chroma_db" )
# QUERY (run on each user request) retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 4}) llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-5") qa = RetrievalQA.from_chain_type( llm=llm, retriever=retriever, return_source_documents=True )
result = qa.invoke("What does the document say about X?") print(result["result"]) # result["source_documents"] shows exactly which chunks were retrieved ```
**Where to look when it fails:** `return_source_documents=True` is your first debugging tool — if the retrieved chunks don't contain the answer, the problem is in retrieval (chunk size, k, or embedding model), not generation. `search_kwargs={"k": 4}` is the highest-impact tuning knob: too few chunks misses context; too many dilutes relevance.
**Limits:** `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is fast (22M parameters) but degrades on technical queries with rare vocabulary — swap in `all-mpnet-base-v2` when precision matters more than inference speed. Chroma with `persist_directory` reloads the existing index on startup — add new documents with `vectorstore.add_documents(new_chunks)` without rebuilding from scratch.
**Sources:** [RAG Explained from Scratch with LangChain — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iKzYPBC5c5Y) · [LangChain RAG documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/rag) · [sentence-transformers pretrained models — SBERT.net](https://www.sbert.net/docs/pretrained_models.html)
